title: USDA Announces Forest Service Headquarters Move and Major Restructuring
description_short: USDA announced a Forest Service headquarters move to Salt Lake City and a broader shift to state-based oversight.
description_medium: On March 31, 2026, USDA announced plans to move U.S. Forest Service headquarters from Washington, D.C., to Salt Lake City and reorganize the agency around 15 state directors. The plan closes all regional offices, shifts shared support to service centers, and consolidates research leadership in Fort Collins. USDA said the changes would bring leaders closer to forests and save money; critics warned of staffing and research disruptions.
description_long: On March 31, 2026, the U.S. Department of Agriculture announced that the Forest Service would move its headquarters from Washington, D.C., to Salt Lake City and begin a major reorganization. The announced model replaces regional oversight with 15 state directors, moves administrative and technical work into service centers, and consolidates leadership of the research enterprise in Fort Collins, Colorado. USDA described the plan as a way to bring leadership closer to forests and communities, improve recruitment, and reduce costs. The release said all regional offices would close during the transition and described the changes as future phases, not a completed relocation. The Guardian and Associated Press reported criticism that closing offices and research facilities could disrupt staffing and scientific work. The linked reporting does not show that scientists were targeted because they refused to support administration policy. This draft records the announced move and its stated rationale while separating critics’ concerns from documented motive and outcome.

title: Trump: Robert Maxwell obtains passports for Mogilevich, helps KGB
description_short: Trump: Robert Maxwell obtains passports for Mogilevich, helps KGB
description_medium: A TrumpFile timeline alleges that Robert Maxwell arranged Israeli passports for Semion Mogilevich and 23 associates in 1988, then connects the group to a Bank of New York account it says was used for laundering. Its TrumpFile page returned HTTP 202 in a focused read, and the supplied record provides no independent documentation for the passport or KGB claims.
description_long: The supplied timeline attributes two serious claims to Robert Maxwell: that he obtained Israeli passports for Semion Mogilevich and 23 associates in 1988, and that he connected Mogilevich to a Bank of New York account used to launder money. It further says the passports and account helped Mogilevich expand a criminal network and titles the event as Maxwell helping the KGB. The record does not include passport records, bank documents, court findings or contemporaneous reporting that independently confirms those assertions. Its current draft describes the TrumpFile page’s references as secondary material, including a book, rather than direct evidence of the alleged transactions. The page itself returned HTTP 202 during a focused read, so its full wording and citations could not be checked here. Because the passport, banking and intelligence claims are the substance of the event, they should remain attributed allegations rather than statements of established fact. The supplied material also does not explain how this 1988 account relates to Donald Trump. A reliable account needs independent reporting or primary records that establish what Maxwell did, when it happened and whether the alleged KGB connection is supported.

title: CDC Removes COVID Guidance Draft After Saying It Was Posted in Error
description_short: CDC removed a COVID-19 guidance draft after saying it was posted before scientific review.
description_medium: The CDC posted updated COVID-19 guidance on September 18, 2020, describing evidence of airborne spread, then removed it on September 21. The agency said the draft had been posted in error before technical review and that its recommendations were being updated. Separate reporting alleged political interference with earlier testing guidance; that distinct dispute does not establish who posted or removed this page.
description_long: On September 18, 2020, the CDC website displayed revised COVID-19 guidance describing evidence that the virus could spread through airborne particles and discussing transmission beyond six feet. Three days later, the page was removed. The CDC said the material was a draft that had been posted before technical review and that the agency was updating recommendations. CNN and the Seattle Times reported the posting and removal and quoted the CDC’s explanation. Coverage of a separate controversy over earlier testing guidance reported allegations of political interference, but that is a different episode and does not identify who uploaded or removed the September 18 page. The available sources establish the web-page change and the agency’s stated explanation; they do not resolve whether the draft was posted accidentally or whether outside officials influenced its removal. This narrower account avoids treating the competing explanations as proof of a White House takeover or assigning responsibility to a person without records.

title: Lyn Redwood Scheduled to Present Thimerosal Claims to CDC Vaccine Advisers
description_short: Former Children’s Health Defense president Lyn Redwood was scheduled to present on thimerosal at ACIP in June 2025.
description_medium: In June 2025, CNN reported that Lyn Redwood, a former president of Children’s Health Defense, was scheduled to present about thimerosal to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. She presented at the June 26 meeting. CNN said one citation appeared to reference a study reporters could not locate, and CDC scientists challenged vaccine-safety presentations. Separate reports said HHS hired her for vaccine-safety work but did not identify her formal title. The original slur and specific-office claim are unsupported.
description_long: At a June 26, 2025, meeting of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), Lyn Redwood presented claims about the vaccine preservative thimerosal. CNN and NBC News identified Redwood as a former president of Children’s Health Defense, an organization founded by Robert F. Kennedy Jr. CNN reported that her presentation argued thimerosal was linked to autism and other harms and appeared to cite a study that reporters could not locate. CDC scientists publicly pushed back on presentations questioning vaccine safety at the same meeting. Those details describe what was presented and reported; they do not show that the committee or CDC adopted the claims. Separate CNN and CBS reporting said HHS had hired Redwood for work connected to CDC vaccine safety, but did not establish a formal public job title. The sources support a specific account of her hiring as reported and presentation to ACIP, with attribution and limits. They do not support the original title’s insult or its assertion that she had been appointed to a specifically named vaccine-safety office. This draft describes the meeting and staffing facts without adopting an evaluative label.
